newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ABN BOARD MEMBER QUITS OVER INSIDER TRADING LINK.
newsitem.headline: ABN BOARD MEMBER QUITS OVER INSIDER TRADING LINK.

text.p: The Netherlands' largest bank ABN AMRO Holding NV said on Wednesday its investment banking chief Louis de Bievre had resigned because his indirect link to a case of insider share trading by his wife.

"This case refers to a situation whereby Mr De Bievre's wife in 1992 traded in shares of a listed company at a time when she was aware of certain specific information related to this company based upon remarks made by her husband," ABN AMRO said.
The news is a major embarrassment for ABN AMRO on the eve of its 1996 results, expected at 0700 GMT on Thursday, and for the Amsterdam bourse where De Bievre had been a board member.
De Bievre, a board member at Algemene Bank Nederland (ABN) since 1984, automatically joined the ABN AMRO board after the 1991 merger between ABN and AMRO Bank, said ABN AMRO spokesman Jules Prast.
De Bievre was one of nine members of the ABN AMRO management board and was chairman of the bank's investment banking and global clients division.
The bank said in a statement that De Bievre had informed ABN AMRO chairman Jan Kalff about the case on Tuesday.

It said that in subsequent contacts between the public prosecutor and ABN AMRO's management board, the prosecutor had stated that in his opinion De Bievre's wife, and not De Bievre himself, had been guilty of insider trading.

Prast said the bank had been informed by De Bievre and the Dutch public prosecutor of the matter but would not comment on the name of the company involved or give details on the nature of the insider offence.
"We won't go into the specifics of the case because we don't know them. There's no direct knowledge within the bank about this case," said Prast.

"The case was brought to the attention of the chairman of ABN AMRO yesterday and there have been consultations at board level. We think it's in the interests of ABN AMRO and of every one to deal with this as swiftly as possible," said Prast.
"We regret that we have to say farewell to Mr De Bievre...but any board member would be expected to set an example in his behaviour," he added.
ABN AMRO said the case would not go to trial as the matter had been settled in an out-of-court agreement with the Dutch public prosecutor in accordance with Dutch criminal law.
"As far as we are concerned there is no further action to be taken by us and we would hope that this brings an end to the matter," Prast said.
ABN AMRO said its management board respected De Bievre's decision and regretted that his long and successful career at the bank had ended in this way.
Insider trading prosecutions are rare in the Netherlands. So far only one case has ended in a successful conviction.

In January a court convicted a 38-year-old man for insider trading, fining him 25,000 guilders and confiscating 32,000 guilders in illegal profits earned from insider trading in shares of industrial springs maker Weweler in late 1993.
